name: io.github.Kromatic-Innovation/neumann
title: Neumann
description: Monte Carlo ranges for uncertain plans: project cost, budget, timeline, capacity, NPV/IRR/payback.

tools.name: run_monte_carlo_simulation
tools.description: Runs a Monte Carlo simulation of a model and returns the full range of possible outcomes, not one guessed number. A model is a set of uncertain inputs, the formulas that combine them, and the links between them. The simulation draws random values for every input many times; each draw is a trial, and one call is one run. Use this when you need to know how likely different outcomes are for a plan built on uncertain inputs: a project's total cost or budget (for example from low / most likely / high estimates per line item), a schedule or delivery date, capacity, revenue, or an investment's NPV, IRR or payback. It returns a summary: for each output node (the nodes nothing else depends on, or the ones you list in run_params.output_request.nodes) the mean, the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles (the value that share of trials fall below), the minimum and maximum in the last time period, and the same per period; plus any metrics you asked for, such as NPV, IRR, payback or the chance of beating a target or budget; and a run_id. Pass that run_id to get_simulation_results for other nodes, periods or percentiles. A run that takes longer than about 40 seconds keeps running in the background: you get status running and a run_id, and get_simulation_results gives you progress and then the result. Cost: without an account, 1 of your 3 free runs per UTC day, for a model up to 1,000 trials and 20 nodes; that daily allowance is counted per network address and client, so on a shared platform such as Claude.ai or ChatGPT you may find today's free runs already spent by someone else. Signed in with a free Kromatic account, 1 of 10 free runs per UTC day, for a small model (trials x nodes x periods at most 100,000, and within 10,000 trials and 50 nodes), spent before any credits. Beyond that -- a larger model, or a day whose free runs are used up -- 1 credit for a small run or 5 for a large one, currently $0.50 per credit; buy_credits tops up. A model that is invalid, or over the limits of the tier you are in, is rejected before running and costs nothing. If it fails mid-run, it depends on the tier: without an account the free run is still used up and not given back; signed in on a free run, the free run is given back; on credits, you are not charged.

graph.description: The model. A model has four parts. root_nodes are the uncertain inputs; each one draws a value from a probability distribution in every trial. calc_nodes are formulas that combine values. edges are links that carry a value from one node to another; a formula refers to its incoming edges by id, like {e1} * {e2}. run_params sets how many trials (random samples) and time periods to simulate. A time period is whatever unit the model's author chooses, such as a month, quarter or year. run_params.time_periods is a count, while time_period arguments and output_request.time_periods are indices counted from 0: with 12 monthly periods, index 11 is month 12. Formula syntax is described on calc_nodes[].formula. Common distributions and their parameters: normal{mean,std}, log_normal{mu,sigma}, uniform{low,high}, triangle{min_val,max_val,mode_val}, beta{alpha,beta}, poisson{lambda_val}, bernoulli{p}.

seed.description: Optional whole number that fixes the random draws, so repeating the call gives the same result. Exact repeats are guaranteed only for small runs, where trials × nodes × time periods is at most 100,000.
seed.title: Seed

detail.description: How much to return. summary (the default): the output nodes' mean, 10th/50th/90th percentiles, minimum and maximum, a compact per-period series, and your metrics. full: every node and edge in every period with histograms, cut down with a truncation note if it would be too large for the client. Prefer summary, then ask get_simulation_results for the specific numbers you need.
detail.title: Detail

AggregationRequest.description: A financial metric computed over one node's whole time series in every trial, then summarized as a distribution. Available: npv (net present value), irr (internal rate of return), mirr (modified IRR), payback and discounted_payback (periods until cumulative cash turns positive), cagr (compound annual growth rate), cumsum (running total), terminal_value, and prob (the chance a value passes a threshold). Discounting counts periods from 0: the first period is not discounted. Model an up-front investment as a negative value in period 0. Do not also discount inside the node's formula with PV() or DISCOUNT(), which count from 1, or the first period is discounted twice. cumsum gives one number per trial: the total of the node's values over every simulated period. output_request.time_periods does not shorten it. prob can target any earlier metric, including npv and cumsum. Its mean in the result is the probability, the share of trials that pass. A prob that targets a node directly only tests the node's final-period value. Recipe for the chance that a cumulative total over the first N periods beats X: add {id: total, function: cumsum, target_node_id: <node>}, then {id: p, function: prob, target_aggregation_id: total, params: {op: '>', value: X}}, and read aggregations.p.basic_stats.mean. This works directly when the model has exactly N periods. If it has more, point cumsum at a calc node with formula IF({time_period} <= N, {e1}, 0). {time_period} counts from 1. Use cumsum and prob for totals and probabilities here. A running-total node is needed only for rank_inputs_by_impact and summarize_outcome_scenarios, which measure one node in one period.

id.description: Name for this metric in the result. Must be unique.
id.title: Id

target_node_id.description: The node whose time series the metric uses. Needed for every metric except a prob that uses target_aggregation_id. A prob sets exactly one of the two.
target_node_id.title: Target Node Id

target_aggregation_id.description: Only for prob: the id of a metric listed earlier in this request (for example an npv or cumsum) whose per-trial values are tested against the threshold.
target_aggregation_id.title: Target Aggregation Id

function.description: One of npv, irr, mirr, payback, discounted_payback, cagr, cumsum, terminal_value, prob. npv needs rate, a decimal per period (0.01 is 1%), so a model with monthly periods needs a monthly rate (10% a year is about 0.008 a month); or rates, a list of per-period decimals with at least one entry per period; the first entry is ignored because period 0 is not discounted. discounted_payback needs rate. terminal_value needs g (growth) and rate. mirr needs finance_rate and reinvest_rate. prob needs op (>, >=, <, <=, ==) and value.
function.title: Function

params.description: The metric's settings, for example {"rate": 0.1} for npv, {"op": ">", "value": 0} for prob, {"g": 0.02, "rate": 0.1} for terminal_value.
params.title: Params

AggregationRequest.title: AggregationRequest

CalcNode.description: A formula node. Its formula combines the values on its incoming edges. There is no automatic sum: write {e1}+{e2} to add two edges, or {e1} to pass one through. A node with no formula is always 0, and check_simulation_model reports that as a warning.

id.description: Unique id for this node within the model.
id.title: Id

formula.description: Expression over incoming edge ids in braces, for example '{e1} * 0.5 + {e2}'. Leave it out only if the node should always be 0. Operators: + - * / ^ (power) and parentheses; dividing by zero gives 0. Comparisons == != < <= > >= work inside IF. Functions (any case): MIN, MAX, ROUND, ABS, POW, SQRT, LOG, LN, EXP, FLOOR, CEIL, SUM, PRODUCT, AVERAGE, MEAN, IF(condition, then, else), AND, OR, NOT, PV(rate, value, period), DISCOUNT(rate, period), BINOMIAL, INDEX(edge, k) for the k-th item (from 1) of a list value, LENGTH. Special values: {time_period} is the current period counted from 1 (unlike the 0-based time_period arguments), {is_first} and {is_last} are 1 on the first or last period and 0 otherwise.
formula.title: Formula

CalcNode.title: CalcNode

distribution_type.description: The distribution's name. Which to pick: beta for a rate or proportion (its values lie between 0 and 1, so 2% is 0.02); log_normal for a positive amount that can run high; normal for a symmetric quantity; uniform or triangle when you know hard limits; gamma or exponential for waiting times; poisson, binomial, discrete_normal, discrete_lognormal or discrete_gamma for whole-number counts; bernoulli for yes or no (1 or 0); categorical for a fixed list of possible values; constant for a known value. dirichlet, multivariate_normal and constant_array produce a list of values per trial; read one item with INDEX({edge}, k). Each type's parameters are in this schema's oneOf.
distribution_type.title: Distribution Type

distribution_params.description: The distribution's parameters. Which keys are needed depends on distribution_type: normal{mean,std}, log_normal{mu,sigma}, uniform{low,high}, triangle{min_val,max_val,mode_val}, beta{alpha,beta}, poisson{lambda_val}, bernoulli{p}. Other types are listed in this schema's oneOf.
distribution_params.title: Distribution Params

interval.description: Draw a new value every N periods; in the periods between, this input is 0 (the value is not carried forward). 1 (the default) means every period. 0 means draw once, in the first period after any delay, and 0 afterwards. To keep one value in every period, use sampling_frequency once instead.
interval.title: Interval

delay.description: How many periods to wait before the first draw. Default 0.
delay.title: Delay

sampling_frequency.description: per_period (the default) draws a new value each period. once draws one value per trial and reuses it in every period.
sampling_frequency.title: Sampling Frequency

estimate.description: Optional: the range estimated for this input, kept with the model. When the graph is saved with save_graph, Neumann keeps it and distribution_params in step: a new or changed range re-fits the params, the way convert_range_to_distribution does, and changed params alone work the range out again. If both changed, the range wins. A run ignores this field and draws from distribution_params.

tools.name: rank_inputs_by_impact
tools.description: Ranks a model's uncertain inputs by how much each one moves a chosen outcome, and returns the data for a tornado chart (a bar chart with one horizontal bar per input, the biggest swing at the top). This is a one-at-a-time (OAT) sensitivity analysis: it shows how much the outcome changes when each input changes on its own. Every input is held at its median while one input at a time is set to low, middle and high values from its own distribution (by default its 5th, 50th and 95th percentiles). The tool records how the outcome's average changes. Use this when you need to know which assumption matters most, so you know what to research or de-risk first. It returns one entry per input, ranked so rank 1 has the biggest impact. Each entry lists the input values tried, the outcome at each, and an elasticity score. Elasticity is about how many percent the outcome's average moves when the input moves 1 percent, averaged over the values tried. It is never negative: it says how much an input matters, not which way it pushes the outcome; to see the direction, compare the outcome at the input's low and high values. It returns numbers, not an image. Inputs whose distribution produces a list of values are skipped. It always returns a run_id. It runs the model once per input per value tried, so on a big model it can take minutes: if it is not done in about 40 seconds you get status running, and get_simulation_results gives you progress and then the ranking. Cost: it counts as one run per call, however many times it runs the model inside, and it is charged only if the analysis succeeds. Without an account, 1 of your 3 free runs per UTC day, for a model up to 1,000 trials and 20 nodes; that daily allowance is counted per network address and client, so on a shared platform such as Claude.ai or ChatGPT you may find today's free runs already spent by someone else. Signed in with a free Kromatic account, 1 of 10 free runs per UTC day, for a small model (trials x nodes x periods at most 100,000, and within 10,000 trials and 50 nodes), spent before any credits. Beyond that, 1 credit for a small model or 5 for a large one, currently $0.50 per credit; buy_credits tops up. A model that is invalid, or over the limits of the tier you are in, is rejected before running and costs nothing, and so is a saved graph refused with incomplete_model: no credit, no free run, no run recorded. If the analysis fails partway through, it depends on what paid for it: without an account the free run is used up and not given back; a signed-in free run is given back; credits are not charged.

graph.description: The model: root_nodes (uncertain inputs), calc_nodes (formulas), edges (links; formulas refer to them like {e1}) and run_params (trials and time periods). Same format as run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph, which documents formulas, periods, distributions and financial metrics in full. Give this or graph_id, not both. Only this outline is published here: the full schema is on run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph parameter, and the neumann://catalog resource lists every distribution and formula function. Neumann checks the model against that full schema when you call this tool and names any problem.

graph_id.description: The id of a graph you already saved, to analyse that graph instead of sending it inline. Give this or graph, not both. Requires a Neumann account -- an anonymous caller must use graph instead. If an input in the saved graph has no distribution yet, the call is refused with incomplete_model, which lists those inputs. The refusal costs nothing (no credit or free run is spent and no run is recorded), so there is no need to check your balance: give each one a distribution, save the graph again under the same id, and try again.
graph_id.title: Graph Id

target_node_id.description: The id of the outcome node to measure. Defaults to the last calc node in the model, which is usually the final outcome.
target_node_id.title: Target Node Id

time_period.description: Index of the time period to measure, counting from 0: with 12 monthly periods, 11 is month 12. Defaults to the last period. This measures the node's value in that one period, not a total. For a cumulative figure such as year-one profit, add a running-total calc node with formula {e1} + {e2}, where e1 brings in the per-period value and e2 is an edge from the running-total node to itself with delay 1. Then target that node at index 11. This delayed self-edge is allowed; only loops with no delay are errors. In run_monte_carlo_simulation, use a cumsum metric instead.
time_period.title: Time Period

quantiles.description: A list of points in each input's own distribution to try. Each point is a fraction from 0 to 1 naming a percentile: 0.05 is the 5th percentile, the value 5% of outcomes fall below. Default [0.05, 0.5, 0.95]. Give this or num_quantiles, not both.
quantiles.title: Quantiles

num_quantiles.description: Instead of quantiles: how many points to try, an even whole number from 2 to 10. That many percentiles are spread evenly between the 5th and 95th, and the median (0.5) is added. 2 gives [0.05, 0.5, 0.95]; 4 gives [0.05, 0.275, 0.5, 0.725, 0.95].
num_quantiles.title: Num Quantiles

seed.description: Optional whole number that fixes the random draws, so repeating the call gives the same result. Exact repeats are guaranteed only for small runs, where trials × nodes × time periods is at most 100,000.
seed.title: Seed

detail.description: How much to return. summary (the default): one row per input with its rank, its low and high values, the outcome at each, the swing between them and its elasticity. full: also each input's whole response curve.
detail.title: Detail

tools.name: summarize_outcome_scenarios
tools.description: Reports one outcome's worst, median and best cases from one run of a model. By default, worst is the lowest value in any trial, median is the middle value, and best is the highest value. Those labels assume higher is better. For a cost or a duration, where lower is better, swap them when you tell the user: the scenario labelled worst is the cheapest or fastest case, which is the good outcome, and the one labelled best is the most expensive or slowest. You can ask for other percentiles instead, such as the 10th and 90th, or the 80th for a P80 total. Use this when you want a short worst, typical and best case story. For the range or the odds of outcomes (what range it could land in, how likely something is), use run_monte_carlo_simulation instead; to find which input matters most, use rank_inputs_by_impact. It takes the model inline in graph, or a saved model by graph_id directly, so you do not need get_graph first. If an input in the saved graph has no distribution yet, the call is refused with incomplete_model and costs nothing. It returns each scenario's outcome value and every input's own value at the same percentile of that input's distribution. Those input values are an estimate, not the exact inputs of that trial. It also returns a run_id; a long run comes back as status running, and get_simulation_results gives you progress and then the result. Cost: without an account, 1 of your 3 free runs per UTC day, for a model up to 1,000 trials and 20 nodes; that daily allowance is counted per network address and client, so on a shared platform such as Claude.ai or ChatGPT you may find today's free runs already spent by someone else. Signed in with a free Kromatic account, 1 of 10 free runs per UTC day, for a small model (trials x nodes x periods at most 100,000, and within 10,000 trials and 50 nodes), spent before any credits. Beyond that -- a larger model, or a day whose free runs are used up -- 1 credit for a small run or 5 for a large one, currently $0.50 per credit; buy_credits tops up. A model that is invalid, or over the limits of the tier you are in, is rejected before running and costs nothing. If it fails mid-run, it depends on the tier: without an account the free run is still used up and not given back; signed in on a free run, the free run is given back; on credits, you are not charged.

tools.name: check_simulation_model
tools.description: Checks a model you hold inline for mistakes, before you save or run it, and lists every problem it finds. It looks for loops with no delay, nodes that are not connected, unknown distributions, missing or invalid distribution parameters, and broken formulas. A loop, including an edge from a node to itself, is allowed and is not an error when at least one edge in it has delay 1 or more. Use this when you have built or edited a model and want to fix it without spending a run. It takes the model inline, not a graph_id: to check a saved model, read it with get_graph and pass what that returns. It does not run or rank anything, and it does not say what a run will cost (use estimate_simulation_size_and_cost for that). It returns is_valid and a list of issues. A draft input with no distribution yet (distribution_type null) is not rejected: it comes back as an issue with severity error naming that input, and is_valid is false, so the model is not ready to run until each such input has a distribution. You do not need this tool to learn that an input with only a low-high guess cannot run: it cannot, and convert_range_to_distribution turns the guess into a distribution. Each issue gives the rule broken, a severity (error, warning or info, where info is only a note), a message, and the node and edge ids involved. If an edge points at a node that does not exist, or the model is over your tier's size limit, you get an error message instead of the list. Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs. Without an account, a model over 1,000 trials or 20 nodes is rejected, also at no cost.

tools.name: estimate_simulation_size_and_cost
tools.description: Predicts how large a run of a model will be and how many credits it will cost, without running it. Use this before running a large or unfamiliar model, or to check that an account can afford it. It does not look for mistakes; use check_simulation_model for that. It returns the number of trials, time periods, nodes and edges, the estimated peak memory in MB, a complexity score, the size tier (small or large), the credit cost for an account, and a rough run time in seconds for run_monte_carlo_simulation and for rank_inputs_by_impact (which runs the model many times). Runs over about 40 seconds continue in the background and are collected with get_simulation_results. A run is small when trials × nodes × time periods is at most 100,000, and large otherwise. Accounts have no fixed trial or node limit. That cost is what run_monte_carlo_simulation, summarize_outcome_scenarios and rank_inputs_by_impact each charge for this model. A model with mistakes returns an error instead of an estimate. Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs. Without an account, a model over 1,000 trials or 20 nodes is rejected, also at no cost.

graph.description: The model: root_nodes (uncertain inputs), calc_nodes (formulas), edges (links; formulas refer to them like {e1}) and run_params (trials and time periods). Same format as run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph, which documents formulas, periods, distributions and financial metrics in full. Only this outline is published here: the full schema is on run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph parameter, and the neumann://catalog resource lists every distribution and formula function. Neumann checks the model against that full schema when you call this tool and names any problem.

tools.name: convert_range_to_distribution
tools.description: Turns a low-to-high guess, such as "between 80 and 120, 90% sure", into the exact parameters a model input needs. A distribution is the shape of the uncertainty, for example normal (a bell curve), log_normal (skewed and never negative), triangle or uniform. The low and high values are the edges of the range you are that sure of, not hard limits. Use this when you have a rough estimate and need distribution parameters instead of guessing them: an input with only a low-high guess has no distribution yet and cannot run until it has one. You do not need it for a three-point low / most likely / high estimate: that goes straight into the model as a triangle input (min_val, mode_val, max_val), so call run_monte_carlo_simulation directly. Its reverse is convert_distribution_to_range. It returns the distribution type and its parameters, ready to use as a model input's distribution_params. The distribution_type parameter explains which type fits which kind of quantity. Supported types: normal, log_normal, uniform, triangle, beta, gamma, exponential, binomial, discrete_normal, discrete_lognormal, discrete_gamma, constant and bernoulli. Not supported: poisson, categorical, dirichlet, multivariate_normal and constant_array. For beta, give low and high as fractions (2% is 0.02). Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs.

distribution_type.description: The distribution to fit. Which to pick: a rate or proportion between 0 and 1 (conversion, churn) → beta, with low and high given as fractions (2% is 0.02). A positive amount that can run high (revenue, price, deal size) → log_normal. A quantity equally likely to land above or below its middle → normal. A value with hard limits you know → uniform (flat) or triangle (most likely value in between). A whole-number count (customers, units) → discrete_normal, discrete_lognormal or discrete_gamma, or binomial for successes out of a fixed number of attempts. Not supported here: poisson, categorical, dirichlet, multivariate_normal and constant_array.
distribution_type.title: Distribution Type

min_estimate.description: The low end of your range. Required for every type except constant and bernoulli. Exponential ignores it, but a value must still be sent (any number works).
min_estimate.title: Min Estimate

max_estimate.description: The high end of your range. Required for every type except constant and bernoulli.
max_estimate.title: Max Estimate

percentile_range.description: A single fraction: the share of outcomes that should fall between the low and high ends, which is how sure you are. The default 0.9 means the middle 90%: a 5% chance of being below the low end and 5% above the high end. Mapping hedged words: "very sure" or "almost certainly" is about 0.9; "probably" is about 0.8; if unsure, ask the user. "Could be higher" means pick a right-skewed type such as log_normal, not a wider range.
percentile_range.title: Percentile Range

mode_estimate.description: The most likely value. Required for constant (the fixed value), bernoulli (the chance of success, from 0 to 1) and binomial. For triangle it sets the peak; it must lie strictly between low and high, and defaults to their midpoint. For beta it is used as the peak when a fit allows, but the low and high ends take priority. Ignored by other types.
mode_estimate.title: Mode Estimate

tools.name: convert_distribution_to_range
tools.description: Turns a distribution's parameters into the low and high ends of the range that holds a chosen share of outcomes, by default the middle 90%. It also gives the mean, median, mode, standard deviation and any percentiles you ask for. If you give a threshold, it gives the chance of landing below and above it. Use this when you have distribution parameters, from a model or from fermi (a companion forecasting server from Kromatic, the company behind Neumann, whose estimates carry next_steps.simulate.root_node), and want to know what they mean in plain numbers. Its reverse is convert_range_to_distribution, and the range it returns can be passed straight back to it. Values that do not apply, such as a uniform distribution's mode, come back as null with a note explaining why. Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs.

distribution_type.description: The distribution's name. Accepts every type a model input accepts: normal, log_normal, uniform, triangle, beta (values are fractions from 0 to 1), gamma, exponential, poisson, bernoulli, binomial, categorical, constant, discrete_normal, discrete_lognormal and discrete_gamma. categorical returns no range. dirichlet, multivariate_normal and constant_array produce lists of values, so every number comes back null. This is wider than convert_range_to_distribution, which cannot fit poisson or categorical.
distribution_type.title: Distribution Type

distribution_params.description: The distribution's parameters, in the same form a model input uses, for example {"mean": 100, "std": 15} for normal or {"mu": 9.2, "sigma": 0.6} for log_normal.
distribution_params.title: Distribution Params

percentile_range.description: A single fraction: the share of outcomes the returned range should hold, centred on the median. The default 0.9 means the middle 90%, so the range runs from the 5th to the 95th percentile.
percentile_range.title: Percentile Range

quantiles.description: A list of percentiles to report. Each is a fraction from 0 to 1: 0.05 is the 5th percentile, the value 5% of outcomes fall below. No repeats. Default [0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.95], returned under keys p5, p10, p50, p90 and p95.
quantiles.title: Quantiles

threshold.description: Optional value to compare against. The result gives the chance of being at or below it and the chance of being above it. For whole-number distributions it gives the chance of being below and above it, and notes the chance of landing exactly on it.
threshold.title: Threshold

tools.name: get_simulation_results
tools.description: Checks on, and reads, a run you started with run_monte_carlo_simulation, rank_inputs_by_impact or summarize_outcome_scenarios, using its run_id. Use this when a run tool returned status running or queued: it waits up to 30 seconds for the run to finish, then returns its status and percent done, or the finished result, so call it again until status is completed. Use it also to get specific numbers from a finished simulation without running it again (a finished run keeps every node's and edge's statistics for every period): pass nodes (node, edge or metric ids), periods, percentiles such as 0.05 or 0.95, a threshold to get the chance a value is at least or at most some number, or histogram for the distribution's shape. Without those it returns the summary (or the ranking, or the scenarios). A failed run returns its error and is not charged. Only the caller who started the run can read it, and only with the run_id, which is returned to that caller alone. A run started without an account can be read for 24 hours and only from the same network address and client, because a caller without an account is recognized by them; sign in with a free Kromatic account for runs that are not tied to one connection. Credentials go in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential; no Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs.

run_id.description: The run_id returned by run_monte_carlo_simulation, rank_inputs_by_impact or summarize_outcome_scenarios.
run_id.title: Run Id

wait_seconds.description: If the run is still going, wait up to this many seconds (0 to 50, default 30) for it to finish before answering. Returns as soon as it finishes. 0 answers at once with the current percent done.
wait_seconds.title: Wait Seconds

nodes.description: Ids of the nodes, edges or metrics (output_request.aggregations ids) to return numbers for. Default: the output nodes.
nodes.title: Nodes

periods.description: Time period indices to return, counting from 0. Default: the last period only. Ignored for metrics, which cover the whole run.
periods.title: Periods

period_from.description: Instead of periods: the first index of a range of periods.
period_from.title: Period From

period_to.description: Instead of periods: the last index of a range (inclusive).
period_to.title: Period To

percentiles.description: Percentiles to return, as fractions from 0 to 1 (0.95 is the 95th percentile). Default [0.1, 0.5, 0.9].
percentiles.title: Percentiles

threshold.description: A value to test: returns, for each node and period, the chance (0 to 1) that it is at least this value (or at most it, see threshold_direction), for example the chance cash is at least 0 in month 6.
threshold.title: Threshold

threshold_direction.description: at_least (default): the chance of being greater than or equal to threshold. at_most: the chance of being less than or equal to it.
threshold_direction.title: Threshold Direction

histogram.description: true to also return a histogram (trial counts per value bin) for up to 3 of the rows.
histogram.title: Histogram

tools.name: check_account_and_credits
tools.description: Shows who Neumann thinks you are and what you can still do: your free runs left today and when they reset, and your credit balance if you have an account. Use this when you need to know, before or after a run, whether the next call will be free or spend credits, how much is left, or whether you are signed in -- and when a run was refused for want of runs or credits, so you can tell the user which it was. There are three tiers. Without an account you get 3 free runs per UTC day; you are recognized by network address and client, so on a hosted platform such as Claude.ai or ChatGPT many callers share one identity and today's free runs may already be spent by someone else. Signed in with a free Kromatic account you get your own 10 free runs per UTC day, spent before any credits. After those, runs cost credits. An account created with POST https://neumann.kromatic.com/api/v1/accounts authenticates you and starts with 5 free credits, but it carries no free daily runs -- only signing in with a Kromatic account does. It returns whether you are anonymous or an account, your account id and status, credit balance, free runs left today with the reset time and the size limits that apply to you, the price of one credit in US dollars, and your last 10 credit transactions. With an account it also returns how many models are saved on your account and the three most recently updated, each with its graph_id, so when the user mentions a saved model you can often go straight to get_graph without calling list_graphs. Credentials go in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential and nowhere else; no Neumann tool takes an api_key argument, and a credential that is not recognized returns an unauthorized error. This tool itself needs no account -- it is how a caller without one finds that out. Setup docs: https://kromatic.com/mcp/neumann. Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs.

tools.name: send_feedback
tools.description: Sends a short report about Neumann to the team that builds it. Use this when the user wants to report a problem, a wrong result, a confusing message or a missing feature (including asking you to pass a request or suggestion on to the team), or has agreed to your offer to send one. Send only after the user agrees: when a tool fails, first tell the user what happened and ask, and do not call this tool until they say yes. Good moments to offer: a tool returned an error or a result that looks wrong, the user needed something Neumann could not do, or the work with Neumann is wrapping up and the user might want to say what worked. Offer it as a question, for example: 'Want me to send Neumann's team a short note about this?' The team reads every report. Do not offer after each routine successful call. Put several points in one report: a signed-in account may send 5 per hour and 20 per day, and callers without an account share 60 per hour and 300 per day. Only message is required. Fill in the other fields that apply so the team can act without guessing. Write in your own words. Never include personal data (names, email addresses, company names), the user's own numbers (inputs or results), secrets or keys, or the conversation transcript; describe the task and any wrong result in general terms instead. Add sender_email only if the user wants a reply. If you are signed in, your account id is included. No account is needed. It returns status "sent". Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs.

message.description: The report, in your own words, 10 to 5,000 characters. Say what you tried, what happened and what you expected. Leave out names, companies, the user's numbers (inputs or results) and the conversation itself: write "a revenue forecast", not its figures.
message.title: Message
examples: rank_inputs_by_impact returned an empty list for a model with two inputs, so I could not tell the user which one mattered more.

feedback_type.description: What kind of report this is. bug: a tool errored or broke. wrong_result: it ran but the numbers look wrong. unmet_use_case: the user needed something no tool does. feature_request: a missing option or parameter. confusing: a description, output or error was hard to understand. praise: something worked well. other: anything else (the default).
feedback_type.title: Feedback Type

tool_name.description: The Neumann tool the report is about, for example run_monte_carlo_simulation.
tool_name.title: Tool Name

run_id.description: The run_id the report is about, if a run was involved.
run_id.title: Run Id

user_goal.description: What the user was trying to do, as a general task in a few words, for example "estimate a project budget". No names, company names or figures.
user_goal.title: User Goal

what_happened.description: What actually happened, in general terms, without the user's numbers.
what_happened.title: What Happened

expected.description: What you expected to happen instead.
expected.title: Expected

error_text.description: The error code and message the tool returned, if any. Remove any personal data or user figures it quotes.
error_text.title: Error Text

suggestion.description: What would have helped: a fix, a new feature or clearer wording.
suggestion.title: Suggestion

impact.description: How much it cost the user. blocked: could not finish. workaround: finished another way. minor: an annoyance. none: no cost, for example praise.
impact.title: Impact

sender_email.description: Optional. The user's email address, only if they want a reply and gave it to you. Do not invent one. No copy is sent to it.
sender_email.title: Sender Email

tools.name: buy_credits
tools.description: Charges the payment card saved on the user's account to buy Neumann credits; without a saved card it charges nothing and returns a checkout link instead. One call buys at most 100 credits ($50.00 at today's price); a request for more is refused and charges nothing. When the user asks for more than that, do not call it yet: tell them the limit and ask how many to buy now. A second purchase needs the user's agreement again. Credits pay for runs once the free runs for the day are used up, or for a model too large to run free. Use this when an account is low on credits and the user has agreed to the purchase; to see the balance and the live price first, call check_account_and_credits. When no card is saved yet, it returns payment_status checkout_required and a checkout_url, which the user opens in a browser to save a card before you call this tool again. It returns the credits bought, the new balance, the payment status and, when a card is needed, the checkout_url. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. When you are signed in rather than using a key, the sign-in must include billing access (the neumann:billing scope); without it the call is refused with insufficient_scope and charges nothing, and the user signs in again to grant it. Cost: charges the payment card saved on your account for each credit, currently $0.50 per credit (check_account_and_credits shows the live price). It needs an account, and credits are what a run costs once your free runs for the day are gone -- 1 credit for a small run or 5 for a large one.

credits.description: How many credits to buy: at least 1 and at most 100 in one call.
credits.title: Credits

tools.name: create_result_share_link
tools.description: Creates a public web link to one of your results, so you can hand the numbers to someone who has no Neumann account. Use this when the user wants to send, publish or show a result to another person; to put the numbers in the conversation instead, call get_simulation_results. It works for any run you own: a run from run_monte_carlo_simulation, rank_inputs_by_impact or summarize_outcome_scenarios, and a run of a graph you saved. There is one share tool for every kind of run -- do not look for a separate one. Pass the run_id the run tool returned when the run was made, earlier in the conversation; no tool lists runs, and you do not need a graph_id. That holds for a run of a saved model too: when the user asks to share the run of a saved graph, call this tool directly with that run's run_id -- list_graphs and get_graph return graph_ids, not run_ids, so they are not a step here. Calling it again for the same run returns the same link rather than a second one. Anyone who has the link can open the result without signing in, so ask the user before you create one. delete_run deletes the stored result, which also stops its share link working. There is no way to turn off a link and keep the result. A run made without an account takes two calls, and the run_id is what carries it from one to the other. First call: the caller has no account, so call this tool with the run_id anyway; nothing is shared, and it returns a message asking the user to sign in with a free Kromatic account -- tell the user that. Second call: once the user has signed in, call this tool again with the SAME run_id. Only that second call shares the run and keeps it on the account; signing in alone shares nothing, and a different run_id, or a new run, does not carry the claim. Do it within 24 hours, because a run made without an account is deleted after that. When you tell the user what happens next, say both steps: sign in, then you will share it using the same run. It returns the share_url. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets authentication_required.

run_id.description: The run to share, as returned by any run tool. For a run made without an account, sign in and then call again with this same run_id: signing in alone shares nothing.
run_id.title: Run Id

tools.name: save_graph
tools.description: Saves a model to your Neumann account so you can come back to it instead of describing it again. A saved model is called a graph: its uncertain inputs, the formulas that combine them, and the links between them. Use this when the user will revisit this model -- a budget, a plan, a business case they will update -- or when you want to re-analyse it later without resending it; for a one-off question, pass the model inline to run_monte_carlo_simulation and save nothing. Omit graph_id to save a new graph. Pass the graph_id of a graph you saved before to replace that same graph with this version; the earlier versions are kept, so replacing is not losing anything. An input may be saved before it has a distribution, so you can build a draft model over a conversation; a graph with such an input cannot be run or analysed until each input has one. An input can also be given as an estimated range (estimate: worst, best, most likely) with a distribution_type and no params: the save fits the params to the range. Changing a saved input's range re-fits its params, and changing only its params works the range out again. If a range cannot be fitted, the error estimate_fit_failed names the input and nothing at all is saved: not that input, not the rest of the model, and a graph you were replacing keeps its last saved version. So after that error there is nothing new to read back with get_graph; tell the user which range could not be fitted and fix it. It returns the graph_id to use later, the version_id of the version it just stored, the name, and when it was last updated. Use that graph_id with get_graph to read the model back, with rank_inputs_by_impact or summarize_outcome_scenarios in place of an inline graph, and with delete_graph to remove it. run_monte_carlo_simulation does not take a graph_id: read the graph with get_graph and pass it inline. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets authentication_required.

graph.description: The model to save: its uncertain inputs (root_nodes), the formulas over them (calc_nodes), the links between them (edges) and the run settings (run_params). The same shape run_monte_carlo_simulation takes, except that an input may be saved before it has a distribution: give it distribution_type null and distribution_params {}. A graph with such an input cannot be run until you give it one. An input may also carry an estimate, the range behind it (worst, best, mode): send a range and a distribution_type without params and the params are fitted to the range on save; send only params and the range they imply is stored. Leave estimate out to keep the one already saved. Only this outline is published here: the full schema is on run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph parameter, and the neumann://catalog resource lists every distribution and formula function. Neumann checks the model against that full schema when you call this tool and names any problem.

name.description: A short name the user will recognise later, shown by list_graphs. Use the user's own words for the thing being modelled.
name.title: Name

graph_id.description: Omit to save a new graph. Give the graph_id of a graph you saved before to replace that same graph with this version, keeping its earlier versions.
graph_id.title: Graph Id

tools.name: list_graphs
tools.description: Lists the graphs saved on your Neumann account, the most recently updated first. Use this when the user refers to a saved model that is not among the newest ones check_account_and_credits shows, or to page through all of them; it is how you find the id that get_graph, rank_inputs_by_impact, summarize_outcome_scenarios and delete_graph need. It does not list runs or results -- it lists the models themselves. It returns one entry per graph with its graph_id, name, when it was last updated and how many input and formula nodes it has, plus next_offset when there are more to page through. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets authentication_required.

limit.description: How many graphs to return, most recently updated first.
limit.title: Limit

offset.description: How many graphs to skip, for paging. Use the next_offset the previous call returned.
offset.title: Offset

tools.name: get_graph
tools.description: Reads one graph you saved earlier, by its graph_id, and returns the whole model in the same shape the run tools accept; an input saved without a distribution comes back with distribution_type null and distribution_params {}. Use this when you want to show the user what is in a saved model, edit it before running it again, or run it with run_monte_carlo_simulation, which takes the model inline and not a graph_id. To find a graph_id first, call list_graphs. It returns the graph_id, the name, when it was last updated, and the graph itself: its uncertain inputs with their distributions, the formula nodes, the links between them and the run settings. It reads the model, not any result of running it. After a save_graph error there is nothing new to read: a failed save stores nothing. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets authentication_required.

graph_id.description: Which saved graph to read, from save_graph or list_graphs.
graph_id.title: Graph Id

tools.name: delete_graph
tools.description: Deletes one graph you saved, together with the runs of it. Use this when the user has explicitly asked for that model to be removed, and not otherwise. Confirm which one first with list_graphs or get_graph, because the graph_id is the only thing that says which model goes. Deletion is final as soon as this returns: nothing can restore it, through any tool or any request, so do not tell the user it can be recovered. Neumann clears the stored data within 30 days. Deleting the same graph twice changes nothing and does not extend the 30 days. To stop using a graph without removing it, just leave it saved and do not pass its graph_id. It returns the graph_id, what kind of thing was deleted, the time it was deleted and the date it is purged for good. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets authentication_required.

graph_id.description: Which saved graph to delete, from list_graphs. Its runs go with it. Confirm with the user first: no tool here can put it back.
graph_id.title: Graph Id

tools.name: delete_run
tools.description: Deletes one of your own runs -- one result -- and its share link, leaving the model it came from alone. It works on any run_id you can read, whether the run came from a model you passed inline or from one you saved; afterwards get_simulation_results can no longer read it. Use this when the user has explicitly asked for that result to be removed, and not otherwise. To remove a saved model and all of its runs at once, use delete_graph. Deletion is final as soon as this returns: nothing can restore it, through any tool or any request, so do not tell the user it can be recovered. Neumann clears the stored data within 30 days. Deleting the same run twice changes nothing and does not extend the 30 days. It returns the run_id, what kind of thing was deleted, the time it was deleted and the date it is purged for good. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets authentication_required.

run_id.description: Which run to delete, as returned by any run tool. The model it came from is left alone. Confirm with the user first: no tool here can put it back.
run_id.title: Run Id
